title: Unit 3: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions

topics.name: The chain rule and higher-order derivatives
covers: The chain rule for differentiating composite functions

topics.name: Derivatives of inverse functions
covers: Differentiation of general and particular inverse functions

guide.title: Composite, implicit, and inverse functions: review guide
guide.intro: This unit extends differentiation to functions inside other functions, to curves defined by equations rather than formulas, and to inverse functions, including the inverse trig functions. It also introduces second and higher derivatives.

sections.title: The chain rule and higher-order derivatives
body: Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). Differentiate the outer function, keep the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
Higher-order derivatives are derivatives of derivatives: f″ is the rate of change of f′. In motion, the second derivative of position is acceleration.
points: Read values from a table carefully: h′(a) = f′(g(a)) · g′(a), evaluating f′ at g(a), not at a.
Nested functions need the chain rule once for each layer.
d/dx e^(kx) = ke^(kx), so each derivative multiplies by another k.

sections.title: Implicit differentiation
body: When y is defined by an equation such as x² + y² = 25, differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x: every y-term gets a factor dy/dx from the chain rule. Then solve for dy/dx.
A second derivative can be found by differentiating dy/dx again (with the quotient rule) and substituting dy/dx back in.
points: Evaluate at a point only after differentiating.
Horizontal tangent: dy/dx = 0; vertical tangent: the denominator of dy/dx is 0.

sections.title: Derivatives of inverse functions
body: If f and g are inverses with f(a) = b, then g′(b) = 1/f′(a): the inverse's slope at (b, a) is the reciprocal of f's slope at (a, b).
Inverse trig derivatives: (arcsin x)′ = 1/√(1 − x²), (arccos x)′ = −1/√(1 − x²), (arctan x)′ = 1/(1 + x²). Combine them with the chain rule for arguments like 2x.
points: Find a such that f(a) = b first; then evaluate f′(a), not f′(b).
The derivative of ln x, 1/x, is itself an inverse-function derivative (of eˣ).

example.prompt: Find dy/dx for x³ + y³ = 6xy, and the slope at (3, 3).
example.solution: Differentiate: 3x² + 3y²y′ = 6y + 6xy′. Collect y′: y′(3y² − 6x) = 6y − 3x², so y′ = (2y − x²)/(y² − 2x). At (3, 3): (6 − 9)/(9 − 6) = −1.

misconceptions: The chain rule multiplies by the inside's derivative: 4cos(4x).
Since y depends on x, d/dx (y²) = 2y·dy/dx.
Evaluate f′ at a = f⁻¹(b), not at b.
The inverse undoes f; it isn't the reciprocal.

questions.explanation: Two layers: d/dx [sin(4x)]² = 2 sin(4x) · cos(4x) · 4 = 8 sin(4x) cos(4x) (which also equals 4 sin(8x)).
choiceExplanations: 2 sin(4x) differentiates only the square.
2 sin(4x) cos(4x) misses the factor 4 from the innermost function.
8 cos(4x) drops the factor sin(4x) from differentiating the square.

choiceExplanations: −4e^(−2x) gets the sign wrong: two factors of −2 make +4.
e^(−2x) ignores the chain rule factors.
−2e^(−2x) is the first derivative.

choiceExplanations: 3/4 drops the minus sign.

questions.prompt: If xy + y³ = 10, what is dy/dx?
questions.explanation: Differentiate: (y + x·y′) + 3y²·y′ = 0, so y′(x + 3y²) = −y and y′ = −y/(x + 3y²).
choiceExplanations: The derivative of the constant 10 is 0; it doesn't appear in dy/dx.
−y/(3y²) forgets the x·y′ term from the product rule.
This swaps the roles of x and y from the product rule.

questions.prompt: For x² + y² = 1, what is d²y/dx² in terms of y?
questions.explanation: y′ = −x/y. Then y″ = −(y − x·y′)/y² = −(y + x²/y)/y² = −(y² + x²)/y³ = −1/y³, using x² + y² = 1.
choiceExplanations: −x/y is the first derivative.
1/y³ drops the minus sign from the quotient rule.
−1/y² loses a factor of y when simplifying.

questions.prompt: Let f(x) = x³ + x, and let g be the inverse of f. Since f(1) = 2, what is g′(2)?
choiceExplanations: 1/13 evaluates f′ at 2 instead of at 1, the x-value where f equals 2.
4 is f′(1); the inverse's derivative is its reciprocal.
13 is f′(2), at the wrong point and not inverted.
